# Microbes and their hosts

> *Carrying a microbe is normal. Becoming ill is not. This chapter asks the fifth question of the
> book: how does damage happen, and how much of it comes from the microbe and how much from the
> host's own response?*

## Four words that are often confused {#sec-host-words}

General pathology gave you the vocabulary of tissue injury. Microbiology adds four terms that
students often use interchangeably, although they describe different states.

| Term | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Contamination** | Microbes are present on a surface, not multiplying | Bacteria on an unwashed hand |
| **Colonisation** | Microbes live and multiply at a site without causing damage | *S. aureus* in the nose of a healthy person |
| **Infection** | Microbes multiply in tissue and the host responds | Bacteria multiplying in a wound, with local inflammation |
| **Disease** | The host is damaged enough to produce signs and symptoms | Fever, pain and swelling from that wound |

Infection does not always mean disease. In one Singapore study, 42 of 245 healthy children attending
childcare centres (17.1%) had enterovirus in their saliva with no symptoms of hand, foot and mouth
disease at the time of sampling [@min2021hfmd]. A person who carries and can transmit an organism
without being ill is a **carrier**.

## The microbiota {#sec-host-microbiota}

The **microbiota** is the community of microbes that normally lives on and in the body: in the
colon, the mouth, the skin, the airway and the vagina. Composition differs by site, because each
site offers different conditions. Stomach acid, skin dryness and salt, and the near-absence of oxygen
in the colon all select for different organisms.

Resident microbes contribute to defence in several ways:

- They occupy attachment sites and consume nutrients that incoming organisms would need, which is
  called **colonisation resistance**.
- Some produce substances that inhibit competitors.
- Their presence helps develop and regulate the immune system.
- Gut bacteria ferment dietary fibre the host cannot digest, and synthesise vitamin K and several B
  vitamins.

Disturb the community and the protection falls away. A course of antibacterial treatment, for
example, can allow *Clostridioides difficile*, which tolerates the disturbance, to multiply in the
colon and cause diarrhoea. The same logic applies to fungal overgrowth at other sites.

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "microbes are germs, and germs are harmful"
Children as young as seven already describe microorganisms as essentially harmful [@byrne2011children],
and the idea persists into adult life. The reverse is closer to the truth. Pathogens are a small
minority, and the organisms that cause most human infections are often the same ones that live on us
harmlessly most of the time. What changes is usually the *place* the organism reaches or the
*state of the host*, not the organism itself.
:::

## Opportunity: when a resident becomes a problem {#sec-host-opportunism}

An **opportunistic pathogen** is an organism of low virulence that causes disease when the host's
defences are impaired or when it is displaced to a site it does not normally occupy. Three routes
recur:

1. **A barrier is breached.** Skin is cut, a catheter crosses it, or surgery opens the bowel, so gut
   organisms reach the abdominal cavity.
2. **Defences are weakened.** Neutrophils are few after chemotherapy, cell-mediated immunity is
   impaired in advanced HIV infection, or diabetes impairs neutrophil function.
3. **The microbiota is disturbed**, as above.

A **strict pathogen**, by contrast, causes disease in people with normal defences: *Mycobacterium
tuberculosis*, *Salmonella* Typhi and influenza virus do not need a weakened host. The boundary is
not sharp, and the useful question is never "is this organism a pathogen?" but "what does it take,
in this host, for this organism to cause damage?"

## Where the damage comes from {#sec-host-drf}

The **damage-response framework**, proposed by Casadevall and Pirofski, makes this explicit
[@casadevall2003damage]. It holds that disease is defined by *host damage*, and that damage can
come from the microbe, from the host's response, or from both. Plot damage against the strength of
the host response and different organisms give differently shaped curves.

<div data-island="damage-response" data-src="/diagrams/damage-response.yml"></div>

The right-hand side of these curves is the part students usually find surprising: a vigorous immune
response is not automatically good. You have already met three examples in this book. In toxic shock,
a superantigen activates a large fraction of T cells and the resulting cytokine release causes the
collapse in blood pressure. In rheumatic fever, antibodies raised against *S. pyogenes* cross-react
with heart tissue weeks after the infection has cleared. In tuberculosis, the tissue destruction in
the lung is largely the work of the immune response to bacteria it cannot eliminate.

This is the same idea general pathology teaches about inflammation: a response that protects in
proportion can harm in excess. The immunology block supplies the mechanisms.

## Host factors {#sec-host-factors}

Two people meet the same organism and only one becomes ill. Casadevall and Pirofski group the
reasons under the mnemonic **MISTEACHING**: Microbiota, Inoculum, Sex, Temperature, Environment, Age,
Chance, History of exposure, Immunity, Nutrition, Genetics [@casadevall2018misteaching].

Three of these are worth drawing out at this stage.

- **Inoculum.** The number of organisms matters. For some organisms very few are needed; for others
  many thousands must be swallowed before disease follows. Dose also affects how quickly illness
  begins.
- **Immunity.** Both the specific immunity left by previous exposure or vaccination, and the general
  competence of the defences. Absent or impaired neutrophils, impaired cell-mediated immunity and
  absence of a functioning spleen each leave characteristic gaps.
- **Other conditions.** Diabetes is the clearest local example: among patients with melioidosis in
  Singapore between 2003 and 2014, 56.7% had diabetes, against 19.3% of the general population of
  similar age [@pang2018melioidosis].

## What a microbe needs to do {#sec-host-steps}

To cause an infection, a microbe has to complete a sequence of steps. Anything it uses to do so is
a **virulence factor**: a product or structure that helps it infect or damage a host.

The steps are: reach a surface and **attach** to it; **invade** past the surface, or stay on it and
act from there; **evade** host defences long enough to multiply; **obtain nutrients**, iron in
particular, which the host keeps bound to proteins; and **damage** the host, directly or through
the response it provokes.

Attachment explains **tropism**, the specific sites an organism can occupy. A microbe can only settle
where it finds the molecule it binds, which is why influenza virus infects airway cells and not
skin, and why a strain of *E. coli* that binds receptors in the urinary tract causes infections there
rather than in the gut.

<div data-island="sorter" data-src="/diagrams/pathogenesis-sorter.yml"></div>

## Two meanings of "toxin" {#sec-host-toxins}

Students meet two things called toxins and often merge them. They differ in almost every respect.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-exotoxin-endotoxin.yml"></div>

The clinical importance of the difference is worth stating plainly. Protein exotoxins can be
inactivated and used as **toxoid** vaccines, which is how tetanus and diphtheria are prevented.
Lipopolysaccharide cannot, and the inflammatory response it drives is central to the deterioration
seen in severe Gram-negative infection.

## Three shapes of infection {#sec-host-courses}

Infections differ in how they unfold over time, and the pattern often follows from the organism's
strategy.

| Pattern | What happens | Typical strategy |
|---|---|---|
| **Acute** | Rapid onset; the organism is cleared or the host dies | Multiply fast, transmit, move on |
| **Latent** | The organism persists silently and can reactivate | Survive inside cells or in a site the immune response reaches poorly |
| **Chronic** | Infection and inflammation continue for months or years | Resist clearance; damage accumulates from the ongoing response |

Latency matters at this stage because it explains clinical patterns you will meet repeatedly. An
organism that persists in a site where immune surveillance is limited, or inside the cells meant to
destroy it, can return when immunity falls, sometimes decades later.

## The questions this chapter answers {#sec-host-close}

For every organism in Part II, two of the six questions now have a standard form.

**How does damage happen?** By direct destruction of cells, by toxins, by provoking a damaging
inflammatory response, or by some combination. Ask which dominates.

**How much is microbe and how much is host?** Place the organism on the damage-response curve. If
most of the damage comes from the response, a weakened host may have *less* visible disease, and
treatment that only removes the organism may not stop the damage.
